questions.statement: Read: He pushed his food around the plate and glanced at his phone every minute. What can be inferred?
questions.context: Lucia reads a short story passage in English class where a boy keeps checking his phone at dinner.

options.text: He is anxious about an expected message.
options.feedback: Correct! Checking his phone repeatedly during dinner shows he is distracted and worried about a message, which strongly supports the conclusion that he is anxious.

options.text: He is calmly enjoying the family dinner.
options.feedback: The idea that he is enjoying dinner calmly fails because calm enjoyment contradicts the restless habit of checking his phone again and again.

options.text: He is angry at his parents for cooking late.
options.feedback: The idea that he is angry at his family fails because the passage shows no argument or complaint, only the repeated and nervous phone checking.

options.text: He has already finished all his homework.
options.feedback: The idea that he has finished all his homework fails because homework completion is never mentioned and cannot be inferred from checking a phone.

questions.explanation: Inference means combining stated clues with background knowledge to reach a logical conclusion that the text supports but never states directly in words.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: Marta grabbed her umbrella even though the morning was bright. The radio had warned of afternoon storms. What is the best conclusion?
questions.context: Diego reads a paragraph about a girl who takes an umbrella although the sky looks clear.

options.text: She expects rain later despite the clear sky.
options.feedback: Correct! Taking an umbrella under a clear sky suggests she trusts the forecast she heard, so the conclusion that she expects later rain is strongly supported.

options.text: She simply enjoys carrying heavy objects around.
options.feedback: The idea that she likes carrying heavy objects fails because nobody enjoys extra weight, and the umbrella choice clearly connects to weather expectations.

options.text: She plans to use the umbrella as a walking stick.
options.feedback: The idea that she wants to use it as a walking stick fails because nothing describes walking difficulty, while the weather motive explains the action.

options.text: She is trying to protect herself from sunshine.
options.feedback: The idea that she is afraid of sunshine fails because sunscreen or a hat would solve sunshine, while an umbrella points specifically to expected rain.

questions.explanation: A good conclusion follows the strongest evidence chain, not a single word. Look for repeated clues about weather, habits, or warnings that point to one outcome.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: The final twist surprised me, yet every clue pointed to it. What does the reviewer conclude about the book?
questions.context: Sara reads a book review excerpt where the reviewer praises the ending as surprising but logical.

options.text: The reviewer disliked the book completely.
options.feedback: The idea that the reviewer hated the book fails because praising the ending as surprising but logical expresses clear admiration, not hatred or disappointment.

options.text: The reviewer thinks the book ending works well.
options.feedback: Correct! Calling the ending surprising but logical shows the reviewer believes the conclusion works well, which supports overall approval of the book.

options.text: The reviewer only liked the book cover design.
options.feedback: The idea that the reviewer only liked the cover fails because the comment focuses on plot logic and the ending, not on pictures or cover design.

options.text: The reviewer found the book far too long.
options.feedback: The idea that the reviewer found the book too long fails because length is never mentioned, while the praise clearly addresses story quality.

questions.explanation: Conclusions in reviews often hide in evaluative adjectives. Words like surprising, logical, moving, or flat tell you the reviewer judgment without stating it plainly.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: After the council built protected bike lanes, cycling to school doubled in one year. What conclusion follows?
questions.context: Pablo reads a news paragraph about a town where bike use doubled after new lanes opened.

options.text: Residents now hate bicycles and avoid them.
options.feedback: The idea that people hate bicycles now fails because doubled bike use proves growing interest, which directly contradicts any claim of hatred.

options.text: The new lanes had no effect on anyone.
options.feedback: The idea that the lanes had no effect fails because the sharp rise right after opening strongly suggests the lanes encouraged more cycling.

options.text: Safe lanes encouraged more people to cycle.
options.feedback: Correct! The doubling of bike use right after the lanes opened supports the conclusion that safe lanes encouraged residents to cycle more.

options.text: Cars in the town became much faster.
options.feedback: The idea that cars became faster fails because the paragraph gives no speed data for cars and focuses entirely on increased bicycle use.

questions.explanation: When a text shows a change after an action, infer causation carefully. Check whether the timing, numbers, and context make the link reasonable before concluding.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: This soup is certainly interesting, she said, sliding the bowl aside untouched. What is implied?
questions.context: Carmen reads a dialogue where a customer says the soup is interesting while pushing the bowl away.

options.text: She loves the soup very much.
options.feedback: The idea that she loves the soup fails because pushing the bowl away contradicts love, showing rejection rather than enjoyment of the dish.

options.text: She politely implies she dislikes the soup.
options.feedback: Correct! Saying interesting while pushing the bowl away is polite code for dislike, so the inference that she dislikes it is correct.

options.text: She wants a much larger portion now.
options.feedback: The idea that she wants a larger portion fails because pushing food away signals refusal, which is the opposite of asking for more soup.

options.text: She thinks the soup is simply too hot.
options.feedback: The idea that she finds the soup too hot fails because she does not wait or blow on it, she rejects it, which points to taste not temperature.

questions.explanation: Polite language often hides true meaning. Combine the words with body language and actions to infer whether interesting means delicious or a gentle complaint.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Fill the gap with the best conclusion. The house was dark, voices were whispers, and everyone tiptoed to bed. It was ___.
questions.context: Hugo reads a passage where lights are off everywhere and the family speaks in whispers.

options.text: It is late at night and everyone is going to sleep.
options.feedback: Correct! Dark rooms, whispers, and everyone heading to bed all point to late night, so the conclusion about time is firmly supported.

options.text: It is early morning and everyone is waking up.
options.feedback: The idea that it is early morning fails because mornings bring light and waking routines, not dark rooms and whispers before sleep.

options.text: A loud birthday party is about to start.
options.feedback: The idea that a party is starting fails because parties are noisy and bright, while this house is dark, quiet, and sleepy.

options.text: The family is doing a deep house cleaning.
options.feedback: The idea that they are cleaning the house fails because cleaning involves noise and light, not whispers and turning lights off for bed.

questions.explanation: Setting details like light, sound, and movement imply time and situation. Dark quiet houses with sleeping actions usually signal late night without saying it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: Due to budget cuts, the central library will close on Sundays from March. Which consequence is most logical?
questions.context: Elena reads an article excerpt saying a library will close on Sundays due to budget cuts.

options.text: All students will suddenly read more books.
options.feedback: The idea that all students will read more books fails because reduced opening hours normally decrease access, not magically increase reading.

options.text: The library will buy many more new books.
options.feedback: The idea that the library will buy more books fails because budget cuts mean less money, which contradicts any expansion of purchases.

options.text: Weekend readers will be most affected by closure.
options.feedback: Correct! Closing on Sundays logically hurts weekend visitors most, so workers and busy students lose their main visiting day.

options.text: Nobody will ever visit on Mondays again.
options.feedback: The idea that Monday visits will disappear fails because weekday opening remains, so Monday readers keep their usual access to the library.

questions.explanation: To infer consequences, link the stated fact to real life effects. A Sunday closure most affects the readers who can only visit on weekends.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: The turtle practised each morning while the hare boasted and napped. The turtle won. What moral is implied?
questions.context: Marco reads a fable where a turtle trains daily while a hare naps confidently.

options.text: Natural talent alone always guarantees victory.
options.feedback: The idea that talent alone guarantees victory fails because the talented hare loses through laziness, proving talent without effort is insufficient.

options.text: Steady effort matters more than overconfidence.
options.feedback: Correct! The daily training turtle beating the napping hare teaches that steady effort beats overconfidence, which is the fable moral.

options.text: Sleeping during a contest is good strategy.
options.feedback: The idea that sleeping is the best training fails because the nap directly causes the defeat, so the story clearly criticizes that choice.

options.text: Running races should be banned as dangerous.
options.feedback: The idea that racing is dangerous fails because nobody is hurt, and the focus is on preparation and attitude rather than physical danger.

questions.explanation: Fables teach morals through contrast. Compare the steady character with the overconfident one to infer which behavior the author wants readers to copy.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the better conclusion. For three months he skipped snacks and kept coins in a jar labelled BIKE. Which fits best?
questions.context: Lucia examines two possible conclusions for a passage about a boy saving lunch money for a bike.

options.text: He is patient and responsible with money.
options.feedback: Correct! Skipping snacks for months to buy a bike proves patience and planning, so the conclusion about being responsible fits every clue.

options.text: He hates all kinds of food and snacks.
options.feedback: The idea that he dislikes food fails because he skips snacks for a savings goal, not from dislike, and he still eats regular meals.

options.text: His parents force him to skip lunch.
options.feedback: The idea that he is forced by parents fails because the text shows a voluntary personal goal, with no parental order mentioned anywhere.

options.text: He is careless and wastes his money.
options.feedback: The idea that he is careless with money fails because saving consistently for months is the opposite of careless spending behavior.

questions.explanation: Evaluating conclusions means testing each against all evidence. The best choice explains every clue, while weaker ones ignore savings, patience, or goals.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: What a week! Unforgettable sunsets! I attach ten photos. What can be inferred about the writer attitude?
questions.context: Andres reads an email where a friend writes that the beach trip was unforgettable and attaches ten photos.

options.text: The beach trip was a terrible experience.
options.feedback: The idea that the trip was terrible fails because unforgettable with ten shared photos signals joy, which contradicts a terrible experience.

options.text: The friend lost the camera on the trip.
options.feedback: The idea that the friend lost the camera fails because attaching ten photos proves the camera worked and the moments were captured.

options.text: The friend loved the trip very much.
options.feedback: Correct! Calling the trip unforgettable and sending ten photos shows genuine enthusiasm, so the positive inference is correct.

options.text: The friend never wants to travel again.
options.feedback: The idea that the friend will never travel again fails because happy travellers usually want more trips, not fewer future journeys.

questions.explanation: Tone plus action reveals attitude. Enthusiastic adjectives combined with sharing many photos signal a highly positive experience, not a neutral report.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: Streets flood whenever heavy rain lasts over an hour. Rain has fallen for two hours. What follows logically?
questions.context: Noa reads a science text stating that streets flood whenever heavy rain lasts more than an hour.

options.text: The streets will probably be flooded.
options.feedback: Correct! Two hours exceeds the one hour limit stated, so flooding is the certain logical prediction from the given condition.

options.text: The streets will remain perfectly dry.
options.feedback: The idea that streets will stay perfectly dry fails because it directly contradicts the stated rule linking long rain to flooding.

options.text: The rain will stop within five minutes.
options.feedback: The idea that rain will suddenly stop fails because the forecast predicts continuation, and no clue suggests an early stop.

options.text: Traffic in the city will improve greatly.
options.feedback: The idea that traffic will improve fails because flooded streets normally slow traffic, which is the opposite of improvement.

questions.explanation: Conditional statements support predictive inferences. If heavy rain over one hour always floods streets, then two hours of rain guarantees flooding.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: Every evening he dusted the empty chair by the window, as he had for ten years. What is implied?
questions.context: Irene reads a story where an old man keeps a window seat free for someone who never arrives.

options.text: He runs a small ticket office daily.
options.feedback: The idea that he runs a ticket office fails because keeping one personal seat free is emotional, not a commercial selling activity.

options.text: He dislikes visitors and avoids people.
options.feedback: The idea that he dislikes visitors fails because saving a place shows longing for company, which contradicts dislike of visitors.

options.text: He simply forgot the bus schedule.
options.feedback: The idea that he forgot the schedule fails because daily repetition over years shows memory and devotion, not forgetfulness about time.

options.text: He misses someone who will not return.
options.feedback: Correct! Saving the seat daily for someone absent strongly implies loyal remembrance, most naturally of a lost friend or relative.

questions.explanation: Repeated symbolic actions imply emotion. Keeping an empty seat for years suggests loyalty and missing someone, a classic literary signal of loss.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Identify the most logical ending. Only the maid knew the safe code and she cleaned the study that morning. Who likely took the jewels?
questions.context: Tomas compares two endings for a mystery story where the maid knew the safe code all along.

options.text: The gardener stole the jewels at noon.
options.feedback: The idea that the gardener did it fails because he lacks code knowledge and was outside, so evidence against him is much weaker.

options.text: The wind blew the safe door open.
options.feedback: The idea that the wind opened the safe fails because safes need codes, and wind cannot explain the missing jewels logically.

options.text: The owner simply lost the jewels outside.
options.feedback: The idea that the owner lost the jewels fails because the forced absence of force plus insider knowledge points away from accident.

options.text: The maid used the code to take jewels.
options.feedback: Correct! The maid knew the code and cleaned that room, so concluding she took the jewels best uses every planted clue.

questions.explanation: The most logical story ending is the one that uses planted clues. Prior knowledge of the code plus presence at the scene makes one suspect stand out.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: Battery weak, camera average, but at this price ideal for a first phone. What does the reviewer conclude?
questions.context: Julia reads a product review that lists many faults but ends by recommending the phone for teenagers.

options.text: The phone is perfect in every way.
options.feedback: The idea that the phone is perfect fails because the long fault list contradicts perfection, even though the final verdict is positive.

options.text: It is cheap and good enough for teens.
options.feedback: Correct! Recommending a faulty but cheap phone for teenagers implies it is affordable and good enough for basic young user needs.

options.text: Teenagers will surely hate this phone.
options.feedback: The idea that teenagers hate cheap phones fails because the recommendation assumes they will accept it, showing expected satisfaction.

options.text: The reviewer was paid to praise it.
options.feedback: The idea that the reviewer was paid fails because honest fault listing suggests independence, not hidden payment for praise.

questions.explanation: Recommendations after criticism imply a balance of needs. A cheap but weak device can still suit users who value price over power and cameras.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: When merchants spread word of their golden harvests, the village raised high stone walls. What is the likely reason?
questions.context: Alba reads a historical passage where a village builds walls right after traders describe rich harvests.

options.text: The walls were built as decoration.
options.feedback: The idea that walls were decoration fails because urgent building after harvest news signals protection, not artistic decoration of villages.

options.text: Villagers simply loved hard physical work.
options.feedback: The idea that villagers loved hard work fails because motive matters more than effort, and fear explains the sudden timing better.

options.text: They feared raids after showing wealth.
options.feedback: Correct! Raising walls right after boasting about harvests implies fear of attack, so protection is the logical inferred motive.

options.text: Travelling traders built the walls alone.
options.feedback: The idea that traders built the walls fails because villagers are the builders in the text, while traders only brought the news.

questions.explanation: Infer motive from sequence. Building defences immediately after news of wealth spreads suggests fear of envy and raids, a common historical pattern.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: From Monday, mobiles must remain in lockers during all lessons. What problem does this rule imply?
questions.context: Bruno reads a school notice saying phones must stay in lockers during lessons.

options.text: Phones help students concentrate better.
options.feedback: The idea that phones improve concentration fails because the ban during lessons shows they harmed focus, which is why lockers are required.

options.text: School lockers are too small for books.
options.feedback: The idea that lockers are too small fails because size is never discussed, while lesson distraction is the clear stated concern.

options.text: Phones distracted students during lessons.
options.feedback: Correct! Requiring phones in lockers during lessons implies they distracted students, so the rule aims to restore classroom concentration.

options.text: Teachers want to borrow student phones.
options.feedback: The idea that teachers want to borrow phones fails because the notice orders storage, not collection for teacher personal use.

questions.explanation: Rules imply problems they aim to fix. A locker rule for lesson time strongly suggests past distraction and a desire to improve focus and learning.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: The house feels too quiet now. I keep your drawings on the fridge. What feeling is inferred?
questions.context: Vega reads a letter where a grandmother says the house feels too quiet since the grandchildren left.

options.text: She enjoys the peaceful silence now.
options.feedback: The idea that she enjoys silence fails because too quiet after happy visits expresses loss, not contentment with peaceful solitude.

options.text: She plans to sell the house soon.
options.feedback: The idea that she wants to sell the house fails because no sale is mentioned, while emotion focuses on missing the children.

options.text: She feels lonely and misses the children.
options.feedback: Correct! Describing the house as too quiet after the visit implies loneliness and sadness because she misses the grandchildren.

options.text: She disliked having visitors at all.
options.feedback: The idea that she disliked the visit fails because quiet sadness afterwards proves the visit brought joy that she now misses.

questions.explanation: Emotional inference links quiet houses to loneliness. When joy leaves and silence remains, the implied feeling is sadness and missing loved ones.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Correct the false statement. Passage implies hard work caused success. Which option states the valid inference?
questions.context: Dario faces a test trap where one option repeats passage words but twists the meaning.

options.text: Hard daily training led to her victory.
options.feedback: Correct! It captures the real implication that extra training caused the win, without copying sentences or twisting their logical sense.

options.text: Her easy victory needed no training at all.
options.feedback: The idea with copied words about easy victory fails because it reuses passage vocabulary yet reverses the hard work message completely.

options.text: Extra practice always harms final performance.
options.feedback: The idea that practice harms performance fails because the victory proves practice helped, making this opposite claim logically impossible.

options.text: The coach alone won the race for her.
options.feedback: The idea that the coach did everything fails because the text credits the athlete effort, not a coach doing the work alone.

questions.explanation: Beware word match traps in inference tests. The correct conclusion paraphrases the idea correctly, while wrong options copy words but reverse logic.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: Shops will revive, children will play safely, and air will improve. What is the author main purpose?
questions.context: Nora reads a complex editorial arguing that a new park will help shops, families, and air quality.

options.text: To describe different types of trees.
options.feedback: The idea that the author only describes trees fails because shops, families, and air together show a persuasive case, not mere botanical description.

options.text: To oppose building the park strongly.
options.feedback: The idea that the author opposes the park fails because every listed effect is positive, which contradicts any opposition to construction.

options.text: To explain the history of old parks.
options.feedback: The idea that the author explains park history fails because no dates or past events appear, only future benefits to persuade readers.

options.text: To persuade readers to support the park.
options.feedback: Correct! Listing economic, social, and environmental benefits together reveals a clear intent to persuade readers to support the park plan.

questions.explanation: Author purpose questions ask why evidence is gathered. Multiple benefits listed together signal persuasion, urging readers to support a proposal or decision.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Order the logic and conclude. She watered the dry stem for weeks. One morning a green shoot appeared and she smiled. What does it symbolize?
questions.context: Iker reads a subtle story where a girl waters a dead plant for weeks and smiles at the green shoot.

options.text: She enjoys wasting water every day.
options.feedback: The idea that she loves wasting water fails because her joy at the shoot proves purposeful care, not wasteful use of water resources.

options.text: Plants grow best without any care.
options.feedback: The idea that plants grow without care fails because weeks of watering caused the shoot, proving care was essential to revival.

options.text: Smiling at plants harms their growth.
options.feedback: The idea that smiling harms plants fails because smiling accompanies success and has no botanical effect on plant growth at all.

options.text: Patience and hope can bring new life.
options.feedback: Correct! Patient watering rewarded by new life symbolizes hope and persistence, making this the richest conclusion supported by the ending.

questions.explanation: Literary conclusions synthesize symbol and change. A reviving plant after patient care stands for hope and persistence rewarded, the deepest valid reading.
questions.subject: ingles
